analysis.one_liner: Criminalizes profiteering on essential commodities like oil during declared national economic emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote, after being introduced during the 1990 oil price crisis with 22 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the President declare a national economic emergency — for example, an oil supply shock — and make it a crime to sell essential commodities like gasoline and home heating oil at prices not justified by actual costs plus a reasonable profit. Sellers caught profiteering could face up to five years in prison, $500,000 fines, confiscation of all excess profits, and double damages in lawsuits brought by federal or state attorneys general. An emergency would expire after 180 days unless the President renewed it in 90-day increments, and Congress could end it by joint resolution.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of essential commodities — households buying gasoline, propane, diesel, and home heating oil — who would be shielded from crisis-driven price spikes during wars, natural disasters, or supply shocks. The bill was written with oil in mind: it was introduced two months after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait sent petroleum prices surging.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households buying fuel and essential goods

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a crime, during a declared national economic emergency, to sell an essential commodity at an 'excessive price' — one not justified by the seller's actual costs plus a reasonable profit — with penalties of up to five years imprisonment and a $500,000 fine, plus disgorgement of all excess profits. [S3]
Allows the U.S. Attorney General or any state attorney general to sue profiteers, with double damages (twice all profits earned on the listed commodities) and restitution available. [S3]

Defines essential commodities to include crude oil, gasoline, diesel, propane, kerosene, home heating oil, and aviation fuel, so households and businesses that depend on fuel are the direct focus of the protection. [S3]

Puts limits on the emergency itself: it expires after 180 days unless the President renews it in 90-day increments, and Congress can terminate it — or any commodity designation — by passing a joint resolution, with court review of the President's decisions. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Companies selling essential commodities — oil producers, refiners, wholesalers, and retailers — who would forgo windfall profits during emergencies and face criminal and civil liability for price increases not tied to actual costs.

drawbacks.text: Cost-plus price caps during a shortage can discourage sellers from rushing extra supply into a disrupted market, which could worsen or lengthen the very shortage the law is meant to address. [S3]

The bill concentrates substantial power in the President, who alone decides when an emergency exists and which commodities are 'essential'; courts could overturn that judgment only on clear and convincing evidence of arbitrary action, and only in a single federal court. [S3]
The definition of a 'reasonable profit' and the ban on counting replacement costs would be difficult to apply to real-world fuel markets, inviting litigation and uneven enforcement. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households, the upside is real but conditional: protection from fuel price gouging only when a President declares an emergency, which is exactly when working families are most exposed to gas and heating-oil spikes. The costs are meaningful but manageable — possible supply disincentives, broad presidential discretion, and fuzzy pricing standards — and the bill included sunset and congressional-termination provisions to limit abuse. On balance it was a consumer-protection bill with a genuine design question, not a giveaway.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Lieberman introduced the bill on September 12, 1990, during the oil price spike following Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, with 18 other senators joining as original cosponsors. [S3]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action was ever taken. [S5]
Twenty-two senators — 19 Democrats and 3 Republicans — cosponsored the bill, but it never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any hearing. [S4]
The bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of oil and other essential commodities were better off, because they kept complete freedom to raise prices — and capture windfall profits — during future emergencies. The 23 senators who sponsored the bill got no vote on it at all.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors amid the 1990 oil price spike.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill after it was referred; it died there. [S5]

against.name: Sen. Joseph Biden
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 19 of 55 Senate Democrats and 3 of 45 Senate Republicans signed on — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of any opposition was never recorded.

industries.industry: Oil and petroleum sellers (producers, refiners, distributors, retailers)
industries.note: The bill would cap their prices at cost plus a reasonable profit whenever the President declares an emergency affecting fuel, stripping away windfall profits from crisis-driven price spikes — precisely the mechanism that shifts emergency costs onto households. Its death left them free to capture those gains.

industries.industry: Other 'essential commodity' industries subject to presidential designation
industries.note: The President could designate any commodity of major economic or public-health importance as essential, exposing those sellers to the same penalties if the President declares an emergency. This threat applied broadly but only when an emergency was declared.
